newsitem.title: ZAMBIA: CYPRUS TO PAY $28 MLN FOR ZAMBIAN MINE.
newsitem.headline: CYPRUS TO PAY $28 MLN FOR ZAMBIAN MINE.

text.p: U.S.-based Cyprus Amax Minerals Company will pay $28 million for an 80 percent stake in Zambia's Kansanshi copper mine and spend at least $20 million developing it, the Zambia Privatisation Agency (ZPA) said on Friday.
Zambia on Thursday kicked off the privatisation of Zambia Consolidated Copper Mines Ltd (ZCCM), the country's biggest state-owned company, with the sale of 80 percent on Kansanshi to Cyprus Amax.
Kansanshi is the first ZCCM mine to be sold under Zambia's ambitious programme to privatisate state assets.

"If Cyprus' appraisal programme and feasibility work are successful and the project proceeds, ZCCM will receive a total of $28 million in cash for the sale and retain a significant carried interest in the development on attractive terms," ZPA head Valentine Chitalu said in a statement.
The Kansanshi mine -- in Zambia's Western province -- has been operated on a limited scale by ZCCM and has a delineated resource of some 24 million tonnes of ore at 2.9 percent copper content.
Chitalu said the project would be executed in three stages.
In the first stage, which would take two years, Cyprus Amax would pay ZCCM $3 million and spend at least $5 million on exploration and feasibility studies.
If the project proceeded to stage two, which would be completed within 30 months, Cyprus Amax would pay ZCCM a further $10 million and commit $15 million to drilling and further feasibility studies.
In stage three, the company would pay ZCCM $15 million and provide additional funds required to bring the project onstream.

"If Cyprus Amax elects not to proceed beyond stages one and two, the asset will revert to ZCCM and Cyprus will be required to pay ZCCM 50 percent of any shortfall in committed expenditures," Chitalu said.
Finance Minister Ronald Penza said he was pleased at the conclusion of the transaction.
"I am pleased that this first step in ZCCM's privatisation sees the company forming a joint venture with Cyprus Amax, who are returning to Zambia after a long absence".
Cyprus Amax was a minority shareholder in ZCCM before the former president Kenneth Kaunda's government nationalised the country's mining industry.
Analysts believe that ZCCM's earnings have fallen 33 percent in the past year compared to 1995.
Zambia's privatisation programme is regarded by some economic analysts as Africa's most successful, with the sale of 130 state firms in four years.
The privatisation of ZCCM, which earns around 90 percent of the country's foreign exchange earnings, is seen as crucial to the survival of Zambia's mining industry.
